articles.title: ‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes
articles.summary: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram. In outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German director Werner Herzog has created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters…
body: But suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at the Venice film festival.

The protagonist pair of Bucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.

First they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.

articles.title: Louis Garrel Jokes About ‘Moretti Method’ Acting at Press Conference for Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’
articles.summary: Veteran auteur Nanni Moretti – who has had nine movies in competition at Cannes — is back in Venice after 37 years with “It Will Happen Tonight,” a romantic drama toplining French star Louis Garrel and Italian A-lister Jasmine Trinca (“La Storia,” “Supersex”).
body: “It Will Happen Tonight” is loosely based on the short story collection “Hungry Heart” (Lev Raev) by Israeli writer Eshkol Nevo. Moretti, in his director’s statement, called them “Stories about love, encounters and partings. But also about parents and their grown-up children. And all those bonds that accompany us – more or less quietly – throughout our lives.”
The film reunites Moretti with Trinca who made her acting debut in “The Son’s Room” in 2001, when Trinca was 18, and subsequently appeared in the “The Caiman.”

“It’s been hugely emotional to be back working with him,” said Trinca, who was on the Cannes jury in 2023. “Nanni is the person who forged my idea of cinema. Which is not about being in front of camera with an affectation or a pose.”

“It Will Happen Tonight” instead marks Moretti’s first collaboration with Garrel, who starred in French blockbusters “The Three Musketeers” parts 1 and 2 and will soon be seen alongside Sydney Sweeney in Studiocanal’s “Custom of the Country.”

articles.title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival
articles.summary: In news that might not surprise anyone, Liam and Noel Gallagher skipped the Venice Film Festival press conference for their upcoming Disney+ documentary “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” on Saturday.
body: Variety has reached out to representatives for Oasis and Disney for comment.

Liam and Noel have been press shy as a pair since their reunion, only sitting for an interview together for “Don’t Look Back in Anger” — their first in 20 years. The documentary, which is world premiering at Venice on Saturday night, releases in theaters Sept. 11 before bowing on Disney+ later this year, boasts footage of the band both backstage and onstage.

The brothers also may have wanted to dodge questions regarding rumors about a new tour, with the band posting cryptic teasers on social media the past two days. Noel Gallagher also nodded to a potential 2027 tour in an interview with Talksport recently, saying: “Let’s put it this way: there’s no football tournament on next year, so we’ve got to do something in the summer, right?”
In an interview with Variety, Southern and Lovelace broke down how they went about capturing the Liam and Noel’s reunion, including setting up hidden cameras in their rehearsal space.

articles.title: Aflac Taps Affleck for Commercials to Keep Insurance Customers Quacking
articles.summary: It seems as simple as moving a few letters around, but a new collaboration between Aflac, the provider of supplemental insurance and Ben Affleck, the actor and director, has been years in the making.
body: The star power shines a light on the increasingly competitive nature of advertising from top insurance companies. Aflac initially gained a bigger profile after introducing its duck mascot in 1999, in ads crafted by Kaplan Thaler Group, an independent agency that was eventually acquired by Publicis Groupe of France. The duck flew on to Madison Avenue just months after the debut of the Geico Gecko, another popular insurance mascot.

In the intervening decades, the average consumer has likely encountered Jake From State Farm; Progressive’s Flo and her colleagues Jamie and Mara, not to mention Dr. Rick; Allstate’s Mayhem; Geico’s Cavemen; and Farmers Insurance’s Professor Burke. Liberty Mutual recently expanded its gallery of characters with a fuzzy yellow creature called Liberty Biberty. The challenge for Aflac is that many of the aforementioned insurance companies spend $1 billion or more annually on advertising, with Progressive spending more than $4 billion, according to data from S&P Global and Dowling & Partners.

articles.title: A Long Winter review – hope, desire and subversion in Andrew Haigh’s beautiful winter western
articles.summary: Telluride film festival In a remote Colorado farmstead, a family with a mother gone missing finds a strange buoyancy and freedom as they wait for the snows to melt. Andrew Haigh’s mysterious and beautiful new film is adapted by him from the 2006 story by Colm Tóibín, transplanting the action from…
body: Lester, played by Ebon Moss-Bachrach, is a grizzled, hardened farmsteader in the remote hills whose family has a certain sufficiency from their livestock; he makes a precarious living breeding rabbits for their meat and fur. One son, Tommy (Kit Connor) is leaving for military service, leaving behind his shy brother Mikey (Fred Hechinger); Mikey has secret gay longings, which are nourished by furtive glimpses of glossy Cosmopolitan magazines, with their impossibly exotic visions of big-city fashion and design.

In the midst of one such collapse, Louise simply vanishes in the depths of winter, an event which the shrugging cops and search-party volunteers finally greet by saying that the only thing for it is to wait for the snows to melt to carry on the search, which will be much grimmer by this stage. But what is the truth? The long winter commences, and Lester, utterly hopeless at cooking and looking after the household, takes in a local biracial boy called Jimmy (D’Pharaoh Woon-a-Tai) to do surrogate-wife chores and who excites his ugly homophobic abuse, and to whom Mikey is attracted.

articles.title: Tender Loving Care review – Mike Leigh’s tender and elusive study of love and mortality
articles.summary: Telluride film festival Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a complicated, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on.
body: As so often, the dialogue has that unique Leigh cartoonish quality that isn’t caricature, and the characters often speak with an almost wartime chirpiness in a world of peckers kept up and noses kept clean. This is a perkiness that the thirtysomethings have unexpectedly inherited and modified from their old mum and dad, and Leigh leaves it to the audience to judge the consequent tone of the drama and the appropriate tone of their response.

The setting is Ealing, west London, where, to paraphrase Larkin, people work all day and get half drunk at night, opening up the white wine that’s been in the fridge while worrying about themselves and their family. Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson) is a single woman and social worker who has started dating a fireman (no woke stuff about “firefighter”). She stays calm and polite in the face of aggressive behaviour from clients; her first scene is with an impassive old man in hospital who, asked for his address, recites only a number. He is perhaps a kind of choric spirit in the film, like the homeless man in Jack Rosenthal’s The Chain.
points: Telluride film festival Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a complicated, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on.

articles.title: Act 3 review – queer art history and life reflections from masters of metatextuality
articles.summary: Telluride film festival Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor’s absorbing documentary is a parallel take on their relationship and a nascent drama on artists Claude Cahun and Marcel Moore.
body: Now, they have made a strangely mesmeric, deeply personal, mysteriously stylised film called Act 3, which may itself yet herald a conventional drama about its notional subject. It is structured around Molloy and Lawlor having a weirdly self-aware dialogue about their lives together over 40 years, filmed singly in shot-reverse-shot (was each holding the camera on the other?) but speaking quietly and slowly, as if under hypnosis.

They are talking about their planned film about Lucy Schwob and Suzanne Malherbe, the 20th-century French artist couple who might now be called genderqueer; they styled themselves with the masculine-sounding names Claude Cahun and Marcel Moore, and were lovers who became stepsisters when their parents married. They lived in an attic room in Nantes, which the film psychogeographically reveals is now screen 12 of the city’s Pathé cinema; they frequented Parisian surrealist salons in the 1930s and were arrested for anti-Nazi activism in 1944 in occupied Jersey, but were spared execution due to the liberation.

articles.title: Gallagher Brothers Skip Venice Press Conference for Concert Doc
articles.summary: 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' captures the brothers’ blockbuster Oasis Live ’25 reunion tour, their first live performances after their infamous falling out back in 2009.
body: That Noel and Liam Gallagher would attend the Venice press conference for their new documentary was always a definitely maybe.

In the end, the brothers, reunited after a 15 year split and hot off a blockbuster global tour — the subject of the doc, Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger — did not meet the press in Venice. After posing for a photo call, the Gallaghers buggered off and it was down to Steven Knight, creator of the documentary, and directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace to be here now and roll with it.
Knight, known for creating Peaky Blinders, had never made a documentary before, but said he jumped at the opportunity.

“And speaking first of all to Noel, and he saying that they were astonished at the response to the announcement of the tour, because there was such demand for tickets, it was apparent that only the generation who had originally loved Oasis, but the next generation had discovered the music and had, you know, a strong attachment to it. And the question was, why did that happen?”
points: 'Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger' captures the brothers’ blockbuster Oasis Live ’25 reunion tour, their first live performances after their infamous falling out back in 2009.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson on Chris Hansen’s Objections to ‘Primetime’: “I Hope He Likes the Movie”
articles.summary: The actor touched down on the Lido this weekend for the Venice Film Festival world premiere of Lance Oppenheim's film, in which he stars as 'To Catch a Predator' host Chris Hansen.
body: Chris Hansen is not at the Venice Film Festival for this weekend’s world premiere of a film inspired by his work on To Catch a Predator, but the man still proved to be the center of attention during Primetime ‘s press conference.

Oppenheim said he first discovered To Catch a Predator through parodies of it on shows like South Park. “And when I finally saw To Catch a Predator, I was amazed. Chris Hansen was this like mythological being who had these one-liners that reminded me of Tony Montana [in Scarface ]. His version of ‘say hello to my little friend,’ was ‘have a seat right there.’ I was always fascinated as a young child with the theatricality of the show. I was so confused by it. Was it a prank show? Was it a news show? Was it a circus with Chris Hansen as a ringleader?”

articles.title: 'The Gentlemen's Kaya Scodelario and Benedetta Porcaroli React to Season 2's Most Tragic Death
articles.summary: Kaya Scodelario and Benedetta Porcaroli discuss The Gentlemen and go deep into their characters in Season 2.
body: Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for the finale of Season 2 of The Gentlemen.

The Gentlemen is back for Season 2, and Guy Ritchie 's sophomore season of his gangster series has turned everything up to ten. The action, the betrayals, and the drama. Season 2 picks up with Eddie ( Theo James ) and Susie ( Kaya Scodelario ) now expanding their business into Italy and trying to get Eddie a seat in the House of Lords. But despite the prosperity, things quickly take a turn for the worse when Eddie decides to betray Bobby ( Ray Winstone ), which ends with him waking up in a shallow grave and being beaten nearly to death.
